item.title: Python urllib urlopen timeout Not Working on Windows: Fixing socket.getaddrinfo DNS Hangs
item.description: Why Python urllib.request.urlopen and requests timeout parameters hang indefinitely on Windows DNS resolution (socket.getaddrinfo), why signal.SIGALRM fails on Windows, and how to enforce a hard wall-clock timeout.
item.content:encoded:
While running a batch crawler across 194 official legal and government portals on Windows 11 (Python 3.12.6), our script froze completely on the 14th URL. Even though every request explicitly passed timeout=8 to urllib.request.urlopen and set socket.setdefaulttimeout(8) at startup, the process hung for over three minutes without raising TimeoutError or urllib.error.URLError.

This post documents the exact stack trace when interrupting the hang, why python urllib urlopen timeout not working and python requests timeout hang socket.getaddrinfo happen on Windows, the two workarounds that failed first, and the production fix that brought batch execution down from an indefinite hang to a deterministic 4-second ceiling per host.

1. Environment & Symptom (python urllib urlopen timeout not working)​

  • OS: Windows 11 Pro (23H2, Build 22631)
  • Runtime: CPython 3.12.6 (x86_64)
  • Task: Sequentially fetching 35 statutory HTML pages (urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=8))

Here is the minimal script that reproduced the freeze whenever the batch encountered a misconfigured or unreachable government nameserver:

import socket
import urllib.request

socket.setdefaulttimeout(8.0)

req = urllib.request.Request(
    "https://unreachable-portal.example.gov.gn/",
    headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0"},
)
# Expected: raise urllib.error.URLError after 8 seconds
# Actual on Windows: hangs for 45~180+ seconds
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=8.0) as resp:
    html = resp.read()

When we sent KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl+C) after waiting 90 seconds, Python printed the following traceback:

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "D:\workspace\tools\check_urls.py", line 19, in <module>
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=8.0) as resp:
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\urllib\request.py", line 215, in urlopen
    return opener.open(url, data, timeout)
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\urllib\request.py", line 515, in open
    response = self._open(req, data)
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\urllib\request.py", line 532, in _open
    result = self._call_chain(self.handle_open, protocol, protocol + '_open', req)
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\urllib\request.py", line 492, in _call_chain
    result = func(*args)
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\urllib\request.py", line 1392, in https_open
    return self.do_open(http.client.HTTPSConnection, req,
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\urllib\request.py", line 1344, in do_open
    h.request(req.get_method(), req.selector, req.data, headers,
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\http\client.py", line 1336, in request
    self._send_request(method, url, body, headers, encode_chunked)
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\http\client.py", line 1382, in _send_request
    self.endheaders(body, encode_chunked=encode_chunked)
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\http\client.py", line 1331, in endheaders
    self._send_output(message_body, encode_chunked=encode_chunked)

    self.send(msg)
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\http\client.py", line 1035, in send
    self.connect()
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\http\client.py", line 1470, in connect
    super().connect()
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\http\client.py", line 1001, in connect
    self.sock = self._create_connection(
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\socket.py", line 841, in create_connection
    for res in getaddrinfo(host, port, 0, SOCK_STREAM):
  File "C:\Python312\Lib\socket.py", line 976, in getaddrinfo
    for res in _socket.getaddrinfo(host, port, family, type, proto, flags):
KeyboardInterrupt

The process was stuck inside _socket.getaddrinfo(host, port, ...), before a TCP socket was even created.

2. Root Cause: Why socket.getaddrinfo Ignores Socket Timeouts (python timeout on dns resolution windows)​

In Python's standard library (socket.create_connection), connecting to a remote host happens in two distinct steps:

  1. Name Resolution (_socket.getaddrinfo): Asks the OS resolver to translate the hostname into IPv4/IPv6 addresses.
  2. Socket Creation & Handshake (sock.settimeout(timeout) -> sock.connect(sa)): Creates the socket descriptor, applies the timeout parameter you passed to urlopen or requests.get, and initiates the TCP/TLS handshake.

Because sock.settimeout(timeout) is only applied after getaddrinfo() returns, the timeout parameter in urllib.request.urlopen(..., timeout=8) and requests.get(..., timeout=(3, 8)) only governs connect() and recv(). It has zero effect on DNS resolution.

On Windows, _socket.getaddrinfo calls the synchronous Win32 GetAddrInfoW API (ws2_32.dll). When a foreign government domain has broken authoritative nameservers that drop UDP packets without sending SERVFAIL, Windows retries across IPv4 (A) and IPv6 (AAAA) records with multi-second backoffs, blocking the calling C thread for 30 to 75+ seconds per URL.

3. Failed Attempts​

Failed Attempt 1: Lowering socket.setdefaulttimeout(3.0)​

We initially added socket.setdefaulttimeout(3.0) at the top of the script. As shown in the traceback above, setdefaulttimeout sets the default timeout for newly instantiated socket.socket objects—it does not configure the OS DNS resolver (GetAddrInfoW). The script still hung in _socket.getaddrinfo.

Failed Attempt 2: Using signal.SIGALRM to Interrupt urlopen​

Many Linux troubleshooting answers suggest wrapping urlopen in signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, handler) and signal.alarm(5). Running that on Windows immediately fails:

AttributeError: module 'signal' has no attribute 'SIGALRM'

Even on POSIX systems, SIGALRM cannot reliably interrupt a blocking C call inside getaddrinfo until the libc resolver yields control back to the Python interpreter.

Failed Attempt 3: with ThreadPoolExecutor() as ex: Context Manager​

Next, we wrapped urlopen in a with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1) as ex: block and called future.result(timeout=5). While future.result(timeout=5) raised concurrent.futures.TimeoutError after 5 seconds, the with block itself still hung on exit! Why? Because ThreadPoolExecutor.__exit__() calls executor.shutdown(wait=True) by default, waiting for the stuck getaddrinfo worker thread to finish before exiting the with statement.

4. Clean Fix: Non-Blocking Shutdown with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor (concurrent.futures ThreadPoolExecutor timeout urlopen)​

To enforce a true wall-clock timeout in pure Python on Windows, you must call executor.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True) (available in Python 3.9+) instead of using the with context manager:

import concurrent.futures
import urllib.request

def _fetch_raw(url: str, timeout: float) -> bytes:
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        url,
        headers={"User-Agent": "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)"},
    )
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as resp:
        return resp.read()

def fetch_with_hard_timeout(url: str, timeout: float = 5.0) -> bytes:
    """Enforces a hard wall-clock timeout including Windows DNS getaddrinfo()."""
    executor = concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1)
    future = executor.submit(_fetch_raw, url, timeout)
    try:
        return future.result(timeout=timeout)
    except concurrent.futures.TimeoutError as exc:
        raise TimeoutError(f"Hard timeout ({timeout}s) exceeded for {url}") from exc
    finally:
        # Critical: wait=False prevents blocking on a hung getaddrinfo() C thread
        executor.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)

For CLI batch pipelines on Windows 10/11 where spawning orphan threads for dozens of dead domains is undesirable, invoking Windows' built-in curl.exe (which uses its own asynchronous resolver thread and enforces --max-time across DNS + TCP + TLS) is an equally clean alternative:

import subprocess

def fetch_via_curl(url: str, max_time_sec: int = 5) -> bytes:
    proc = subprocess.run(
        ["curl.exe", "-sS", "-L", "--connect-timeout", "3", "-m", str(max_time_sec), url],
        capture_output=True,
        timeout=max_time_sec + 2,
        check=True,
    )
    return proc.stdout

Verification Result: Auditing 35 international legal portals (including 9 dead or firewalled hosts) dropped from hanging indefinitely (>180s) to completing all 35 checks in 18.4 seconds (<= 4.0s per unreachable domain).

5. Bonus Pitfall: python strip null bytes x00 utf-16 html decode on Legacy Portals​

Once our crawler stopped hanging, one downloaded statute page (bdlaws.minlaw.gov.bd, 282,674 bytes) saved cleanly to disk, yet every regex search (re.search(r"Police Act", text)) returned None even though the text looked normal in a browser.

Inspecting the raw bytes revealed why:

raw = open("BGD_1.html", "rb").read(40)
print(raw)
# b'<!\x00D\x00O\x00C\x00T\x00Y\x00P\x00E\x00 \x00h\x00t\x00m\x00l\x00>\x00'

Because read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") keeps ASCII NUL bytes (\x00), the decoded Python string became "<\x00!\x00D\x00O\x00C\x00...", inserting a \x00 between every character and breaking every multi-character regex!

Fix: BOM Detection & Null-Byte Normalization Before Decoding​

from pathlib import Path

def decode_html_safely(path: Path) -> str:
    raw = path.read_bytes()
    if raw.startswith((b"\xff\xfe", b"\xfe\xff")):
        return raw.decode("utf-16", errors="ignore")
    # Handle hybrid responses containing interleaved UTF-16LE null bytes without BOM
    if b"\x00" in raw:
        raw = raw.replace(b"\x00", b"")
    return raw.decode("utf-8", errors="ignore")

Stripping interleaved \x00 bytes before UTF-8 decoding immediately restored full-text extraction across all legacy statutory portals.

item.title: Air Combat Replanning #3: Deterministic JCS & Ed25519 Frag Fix
item.description: Zero-dependency RFC 8785 JCS implementation, overcoming 0.7 KB envelope fragmentation defect (A-01) and resolving signed delta benchmark distortion (B-05).
item.content:encoded:
This is the third installment in the engineering series on the Air Combat Dynamic Mission Replanning System (SDC). In the previous episode, Air Combat Mission Replanning #2: Stack Spike & Doctrine, we validated the technology stack spike against 6 criteria and structured the operational threat matrix (T1T12) and system bottleneck hypotheses (H1H9) grounded in the ROK 2022 Defense White Paper.

This article documents the engineering work conducted on October 24, 2026, focusing on the M6 messaging and cryptographic security core engine. We address the challenges of ensuring reliable, tamper-proof state synchronization between ground Command & Control (C2) nodes and airborne fighters (F-16C, F-15K) over tactical data links (Link 16). We detail our zero-dependency implementation of RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) to eliminate cross-runtime (.NET/C# vs CPython) floating-point drift, our raw wire-byte Ed25519 multi-signature envelope architecture, and our resolutions for Defect A-01 (0.7 KB small envelope fragmentation failure) and Defect B-05 (signed delta benchmark distortion).

Figure 1: RFC 8785 deterministic JCS canonical hashing pipeline, Ed25519 raw wire-byte cryptographic envelope, and Link 16 MTU fragmentation architecture.

1. Target & Architecture​

1.1 State Synchronization Under Tactical Data Link Constraints​

In our dynamic mission replanning system (SDC), Airspace Control Orders (ACO), threat circular zones (THREAT), flight mission plans (sdc.plan/0), and delta replan packages (sdc.change/0) must be exchanged between ground C2 and airborne strike packages within strict sub-second latency bounds. Over lossy, bandwidth-constrained tactical radio links (Link 16, MTU 1,024 Bytes), the architecture had to satisfy four core engineering requirements:

  1. Zero-Drift State Verification (H2 / I4 Invariant):
    • Ground and airborne nodes must verify that flight plans match not only by integer revision (version), but through a cryptographically strict content hash: plan_sha256 = SHA-256(JCS(plan)).
  2. Cross-Runtime Determinism:
    • The system must yield identical byte-level canonical outputs across research prototypes (CPython 3.12) and operational embedded avionics targets (.NET 8 / C# or C++), completely eliminating floating-point serialization discrepancies and dictionary key ordering mismatches.
  3. Multi-Role Cryptographic Verification (I5 Delegation):
    • Replan changes require multi-signature envelopes (sdc.envelope/0) matching change severity grades (Grade A: target coordinate updates, Grade B: waypoint modifications, Grade C: stores/weapons reassignment).
    • A single Ed25519 key signing as both planner and approver (self-approval) must be mechanically rejected (MISSING_APPROVAL).
  4. Link 16 MTU Budgeting:
    • High-urgency Grade A updates (~0.7 KB) must fit within a single 1,024-byte Link 16 packet without chunking overhead.
    • Large multi-waypoint replans (Grade B, ~1.7 KB) must be deterministically partitioned into ~600-byte payload chunks (sdc.frag/0) with out-of-order reassembly and 60-second assembly timeouts.
         [Ground C2 Planner & Approver]                   [F-16C / F-15K Cockpit]
  +-----------------------------------------+       +-----------------------------------------+
  |  sdc.change/0 (Grade A/B/C)             |       |  sdc.envelope/0 Reception               |
  |  - JSON Patch delta                     |       |  - Ed25519 multi-signature verification |
  |  - Raw Wire Bytes Serialization         |       |  - Delegation table key & role check    |
  |  - Ed25519 Multi-Signatures             |       |  - plan_sha256 JCS state comparison     |
  +--------------------+--------------------+       +--------------------+--------------------+
                       |                                                 ^
                       v                                                 |
  +--------------------+--------------------+       +--------------------+--------------------+
  |  MTU Boundary Guard (1,024 Bytes)       |       |  Fragment Reassembly (from_fragments)   |
  |  - <= 1024 B: Atomic Single Packet      |       |  - set_sha256 integrity verification    |
  |  - > 1024 B : Chunk to sdc.frag/0       |       |  - 60s timeout reassembly buffer        |
  +--------------------+--------------------+       +--------------------+--------------------+
                       |                                                 ^
                       +-----------[ Link 16 Tactical Radio ]------------+

2. Real Errors & Pitfalls​

During the implementation and Monte Carlo testing of module M6 (src/sdc/m6.py), we encountered two critical engineering pitfalls.

2.1 Defect A-01: Single-Packet Fragmentation Trap (< 0.7 KB Envelope Rejection)​

  • Date Recorded: 2026-10-24
  • Component: M6 Fragmentation Engine (to_fragments)
  • Symptoms:
    • A Grade A change envelope (1 target coordinate update + 1 Ed25519 signature) serializes to approximately 655~700 Bytes, well below the 1,024-byte Link 16 limit.
    • However, when passed to the fragmentation module, the envelope was either erroneously partitioned into a single-item fragment set (sdc.frag/0), or aborted with a runtime exception: ValueError: Invalid chunk count.
  • Raw Root-Cause Code: 
    # [DEFECTIVE IMPLEMENTATION]
    def to_fragments(envelope_bytes: bytes, set_id: str, max_msg_bytes: int) -> list[dict]:
        parts = [envelope_bytes[i:i + chunk] for i in range(0, len(envelope_bytes), chunk)]
        # Defect: Artificially rejecting chunk count == 1 as an error
        if len(parts) <= 1:
            raise ValueError("Invalid fragmentation: chunk count must be greater than 1")
        return [...]
  • Consequences:
    • Any upper-layer pipeline invoking to_fragments() without a pre-check failed immediately on all high-priority Grade A coordinate updates.
    • Furthermore, wrapping single-message payloads into sdc.frag/0 imposed unnecessary Base64 encoding and header overheads (set_id, index, count, set_sha256), triggering avoidable reassembly timeout risks under packet loss.

2.2 Defect B-05: Delta vs Full-Plan Benchmark Distortion (H9 Collapse Risk)​

  • Date Recorded: 2026-10-24 (Discovered) $\rightarrow$ 2026-10-27 (Corrected in System Requirements)
  • Component: System Bottleneck Hypothesis H9 (Bandwidth conservation via delta updates)
  • Symptoms:
    • Preliminary empirical measurements in technical feasibility study F1/F3 indicated that JSON Patch deltas yielded no size benefit over full plans: Unsigned Full Plan = 526 Bytes vs Delta Envelope = 811 Bytes.
    • This counter-intuitive measurement threatened to invalidate our architectural justification for delta-based in-flight replanning.
  • Root Cause Analysis:
    • The test harness had conducted an asymmetrical, unfair comparison: an unsigned raw flight plan (526 Bytes) was benchmarked against a cryptographically signed delta envelope containing two 64-byte Ed25519 signatures, Base64 strings, and envelope metadata (811 Bytes).
    • In military avionics, full flight plans transmitted in-flight must also be sealed within signed envelopes. Benchmarking them under identical security preconditions reversed the conclusion.
[Distorted Comparison (Root of B-05)]
  - Raw Unsigned Flight Plan : 526 Bytes  <-- Unfair basis
  - Signed Delta Envelope    : 811 Bytes  [False Inversion!]

[Apples-to-Apples Cryptographic Comparison (Corrected)]
  - Signed Full Plan Envelope : 920 Bytes
  - Signed Grade A Delta      : 811 Bytes  (109 Bytes smaller, 1 single packet)
  - Signed Grade B Delta (10 WPs): 1,740 Bytes (3 fragments)

3. Deep Root Cause & Clean Fix​

3.1 Zero-Dependency RFC 8785 JCS Engine Implementation​

To achieve deterministic hashing across disparate runtimes without external dependencies, we implemented RFC 8785 directly within src/sdc/m6.py.

Figure 2: Standard CPython vs RFC 8785 ECMAScript float canonicalization, Appendix B 24 test vector verification, and UTF-16 code-unit property sorting.

1) ECMAScript Number Formatting (_jcs_number)​

Standard Python json.dumps() preserves trailing zeros (6000.0 $\rightarrow$ "6000.0") and produces negative zero (-0.0). RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3 strictly mandates ECMAScript Number.prototype.toString() conventions:

  • Integer-valued floats (6000.0) must strip decimal components ("6000").
  • Negative zero (-0.0) must normalize to "0".
  • Exponential notation is restricted: fixed point is required when exponent $n$ satisfies $k \le n \le 21$ and leading zero padding when $-6 < n \le 0$; scientific notation is applied only outside these boundaries (1e+21).
def _jcs_number(x) -> str:
    """ECMAScript Number.prototype.toString canonicalization (RFC 8785 §3.2.2.3)."""
    x = float(x)
    if not math.isfinite(x):
        raise ValueError("JCS: NaN and Infinity are not allowed")
    if x == 0:
        return "0"
    mant, _, exp = repr(abs(x)).partition("e")
    ip, _, fp = mant.partition(".")
    s, point = ip + fp, len(ip) + (int(exp) if exp else 0)
    stripped = s.lstrip("0")
    point -= len(s) - len(stripped)
    s = stripped.rstrip("0")
    k, n = len(s), point  # Value = 0.s × 10^n
    if k <= n <= 21:
        out = s + "0" * (n - k)
    elif 0 < n <= 21:
        out = s[:n] + "." + s[n:]
    elif -6 < n <= 0:
        out = "0." + "0" * (-n) + s
    else:
        e = n - 1
        out = s[0] + ("." + s[1:] if k > 1 else "") + "e" + ("+" if e >= 0 else "-") + str(abs(e))
    return ("-" if x < 0 else "") + out

2) UTF-16 Code-Unit Key Sorting (Surrogate Pair Trap Avoidance)​

Sorting dictionary keys by standard Unicode code points violates RFC 8785 §3.2.3 because code-point sorting places Astral Plane characters (such as emojis or extended symbols with surrogate pairs) after Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP) characters. We resolved this by encoding keys to UTF-16 BE:

# RFC 8785 §3.2.3: Sort keys by UTF-16 code units
keys = sorted(value, key=lambda k: k.encode("utf-16-be"))
return "{" + ",".join(_jcs_string(k) + ":" + _jcs(value[k]) for k in keys) + "}"
  • Verification: Sorting {"｡": 1, "\U0001f600": 2, "a": 3}: standard Python sort puts ｡ (U+FF61) before \U0001f600 (U+1F600). However, under UTF-16 code-unit sorting, the high surrogate 0xD83D of \U0001f600 precedes 0xFF61, deterministically producing {"a":3,"\U0001f600":2,"｡":1}.

3) RFC 8785 Appendix B IEEE-754 Full Vector Verification​

We extracted all 24 IEEE-754 test vectors from RFC 8785 Appendix B—including subnormals (5e-324, -5e-324), maximum finite doubles (1.7976931348623157e+308), precision boundaries (9007199254740992), and fractions (9.999999999999997e-7). Our test suite (test_jcs_numbers_rfc8785_appendix_b) passed 24 out of 24 vectors (100% bit-exact conformance).

3.2 Raw Wire-Byte Signing Envelope Architecture​

To eliminate signature verification breakage across varying runtime platforms, we established the rule that signatures are generated directly over the exact transmitted UTF-8 byte stream of the body string, rather than re-canonicalized runtime objects:

def dumps(obj) -> str:
    """Strict serialization: no whitespace, preserved UTF-8."""
    return json.dumps(obj, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":"), allow_nan=False)

def seal(body: dict, signers: list[tuple[str, Ed25519PrivateKey]]) -> dict:
    """Serializes body once; all signers sign the identical raw byte sequence."""
    raw = dumps(body)
    data = raw.encode("utf-8")
    sigs = [{"key_id": kid, "sig": base64.b64encode(key.sign(data)).decode()} for kid, key in signers]
    return {"schema": "sdc.envelope/0", "body": raw, "sigs": sigs}

Because receiving nodes extract envelope["body"].encode("utf-8") prior to JSON parsing, the Ed25519 signature remains valid regardless of whether the receiving runtime parses numbers as 6000 or 6000.0.

3.3 Defect Resolution: A-01 and B-05​

Figure 3: Clean guard fix for Defect A-01 (single-packet MTU passthrough) and fair cryptographic envelope comparison for Defect B-05.

1) A-01 Fragmentation Guard Patch (src/sdc/m6.py)​

We re-architected to_fragments() with an explicit guard clause:

def to_fragments(envelope_bytes: bytes, set_id: str, max_msg_bytes: int) -> list[dict]:
    """Splits envelope bytes into chunks. Each serialized chunk <= max_msg_bytes."""
    # [Clean Fix] If envelope fits in a single message, notify caller to send directly
    if len(envelope_bytes) <= max_msg_bytes:
        raise ValueError("fits in one message; send the envelope as is")
    
    digest = hashlib.sha256(envelope_bytes).hexdigest()
    head = {"schema": "sdc.frag/0", "set_id": set_id, "index": 9999, "count": 9999, "set_sha256": digest, "data": ""}
    chunk = (max_msg_bytes - len(dumps(head).encode("utf-8"))) // 4 * 3
    if chunk <= 0:
        raise ValueError("max_msg_bytes too small")
    parts = [envelope_bytes[i:i + chunk] for i in range(0, len(envelope_bytes), chunk)]
    return [{"schema": "sdc.frag/0", "set_id": set_id, "index": i, "count": len(parts), "set_sha256": digest,
             "data": base64.b64encode(p).decode()} for i, p in enumerate(parts)]

The dispatch layer verifies len(env_bytes) ≤ 1024 and transmits sdc.envelope/0 atomically without calling to_fragments(). High-urgency Grade A coordinate updates are guaranteed single-packet delivery.

2) B-05 Envelope Parity & Break-Even Boundary​

Under identical dual-signed Ed25519 envelopes:

  • Grade A Target Update: Signed Delta Envelope (811 Bytes, 1 packet) vs Signed Full Plan (920 Bytes, 1 packet) $\rightarrow$ 109 Bytes saved (11.8% bandwidth reduction).
  • Break-Even Analysis: Delta updates retain bandwidth superiority as long as the modified waypoints do not exceed 63% to 70% of total route waypoints.
  • S4 Lossy Environment (30% Packet Drop Rate) Simulation:
    • Full plan transmission (3 chunks): 18.6% unconfirmed rate due to packet fragmentation loss.
    • JSON Patch delta transmission: 0.8% unconfirmed rate (23x reliability improvement).

4. Verification & Quality Metrics​

Following implementation and defect resolution:

  1. 87/87 M6 Unit Tests Passing:
    • tests/test_m6.py: Verified multi-signature signing, tampered body detection, unknown key rejection, RFC 8785 24-sample bit matching, UTF-16 code unit ordering, and out-of-order fragment reassembly.
  2. 100% Branch Coverage:
    • coverage run -m pytest tests/test_m6.py confirmed 100.0% branch coverage (42/42 branches) for src/sdc/m6.py.
  3. Cross-Platform Conformance Vectors (vectors_v0.json):
    • Staged a 25 KB canonical test suite (vectors_v0.json) covering JCS edge cases, Ed25519 signatures, and out-of-order chunk assembly to guarantee cross-language parity for future .NET implementations.

5. Next Steps​

With M6 messaging and cryptographic determinism established, our tactical communication pipeline is hardened against serialization drifts and packet loss. In the next episode:

  • [EP. 04] 2026-10-24 (2): 5 Operational Scenarios (S1S5) and I1I5 Safety Invariant Verification Engine
  • Implementing 27 safety rejection reason codes across operational, airspace, and terrain boundaries,
  • Enforcing terrain elevation clearance (DEM) and radar viewshed safety gates,
  • Validating 57 synthetic Q5 test vectors with 100% pass rates.

item.content:encoded:
This is the second installment in the engineering series on the Air Combat Dynamic Mission Replanning System (SDC). In the previous episode, Air Combat Mission Replanning #1: Architecture & KLM Analysis, we established the multi-tier distributed architecture, overcame the CPython 14.5s latency barrier, optimized GPU memory to 0.80 GB, and numerically validated the F-16C fuel integration model via 4th-order Runge-Kutta (RK4).

This article documents the engineering facts from October 23, 2026, when we conducted Technology Stack Spike (a) to de-risk core feasibility before full distributed prototype implementation. We present the verification of 6 quantitative pass criteria, along with the formulation of Operational Threat Situations (T1~T12) and System Bottleneck Hypotheses (H1~H9) derived from official doctrine analysis.

Figure 1: Architectural overview of Stack Spike (a) verification metrics and the ROK 2022 Defense White Paper-grounded T1~T12 operational threat matrix.

1. Target & Architecture​

Before simulating tactical data links and in-flight cockpit mission computers, we needed to establish whether a lightweight Python compute core (FastAPI / HTTP / Ed25519) paired with a browser-based tactical workbench (MapLibre GL JS) could satisfy real-time pilot and ground command operational constraints. Directly adopting a heavyweight legacy C#/.NET avionics stack introduced substantial overhead; verifying the viability of open web standards was the explicit engineering objective of Stack Spike (a).

The Foundation Design Specification (§6) defined 6 mandatory quantitative pass criteria for the spike:

CriterionTarget SubsystemSLA / Performance BoundaryEvaluation & Pass Rule
Criterion 1Terrain Visualization UIMinimum 30.0 FPS during pan/zoom20s continuous pan/zoom over MapLibre hillshade + 4 threats + route; p95 frame time ≤ 33.3 ms
Criterion 2Message Roundtrip LatencyInter-process transmission & verificationRFC 8785 JSON canonicalization + Ed25519 sign + delta apply + signed ACK roundtrip
Criterion 3Local Grade ClassifierInference latency ≤ 50.0 ms, 0 MB GPUScikit-learn RandomForest pure CPU inference, proving zero GPU VRAM footprint
Criterion 4Automated Test Single LineFull regression suite automationComplete test execution via .venv\Scripts\python -m pytest -q
Criterion 5License ComplianceDistribution license auditFull compilation of registry entries L-001~L-009 across PyPI, npm, and Copernicus DEM
Criterion 6Cost Grid Path Search1,000x1,000 grid search ≤ 2,000 msScikit-image MCP path calculation across DEM slope gradients and 4 synthetic threat circles

Concurrently, we investigated the baseline pre-flight planning delays of existing legacy mission planning environments—namely FalconView and the Joint Mission Planning System (JMPS), using DOT&E FY2011 operational evaluations (A-01: 0.94 hr / 56 min for a single aircraft, A-02: 7.30 hr for a strike package)—to ground our threat-induced in-flight replanning requirements.

2. Real Errors & Pitfalls​

During spike execution and doctrinal data collection, we encountered 5 critical engineering bottlenecks spanning network WAF blocks, headless browser power-saving clamps, protocol state desynchronization, and empirical contradictions with military literature.

(1) HTTP 403 Forbidden Blocks on .mil and DTIC Doctrine Endpoints (D-03)​

To generalize coalition air operations procedures, we sought primary US military doctrine sources: AFDP 3-0.1 (Airspace Control), JP 3-60 (Joint Targeting), and ASSIST military message specifications. However, standard CLI tooling—including cURL, PowerShell Invoke-WebRequest, and Python urllib.request—immediately returned HTTP 403 Forbidden responses:

Akamai Edge firewalls and Department of Defense gateway security inspected User-Agent strings and TCP/TLS handshakes, dropping non-browser automated fetch pipelines unconditionally.

(2) Chrome Multi-Tab Automated Download Drops and File Truncation (D-02)​

To automate document acquisition, browser-driven collection scripts were executed. However, Chrome security mechanisms restricted multiple sequential download triggers within a single tab: only the first PDF stream was written to disk, while subsequent downloads were silently dropped without error propagation. Consequently, several critical doctrine PDFs were either truncated to 0 bytes or completely omitted.

(3) Window Occlusion Detection Triggering 1 FPS Clamping and Telemetry Hang (D-04, D-05)​

To evaluate Criterion 1 (MapLibre WebGL UI 30 FPS threshold), benchmark scripts were executed in Chrome. Whenever the canvas window became partially obscured by other operating system windows or minimized to the background, Chrome's internal power scheduler (CalculateNativeWinOcclusion) flagged visibilityState as hidden, clamping rendering execution to 1 frame per second (1,002 ms cycle):

The measurement harness, awaiting MapLibre's idle event, hung indefinitely within the frozen 1 FPS event loop before terminating with timeout failures.

(4) Fatal Ground-Cockpit Desync via Naive Version Rejection (B-04)​

In the initial implementation of the distributed aircraft simulator (aircraft_sim.py), retransmission handling contained a critical architectural defect. Upon receiving a repeated msg_id, the flight computer evaluated the incoming version against its updated local state:

# [Flawed Initial Implementation - aircraft_sim.py]
def handle_change(payload):
    req_version = payload["body"]["base_version"]
    if req_version != current_plan["version"]:
        # If a duplicate msg_id arrives after local apply, reject immediately!
        return make_ack(status="REJECTED", reason="VERSION_MISMATCH")

Under tactical electronic warfare (GPS / communication jamming T5), this logic led to catastrophic state divergence:

  1. Ground C2 (M2) transmits change request (msg_id=42, v1 -> v2) to Aircraft (M4).
  2. Aircraft M4 applies the delta, updates its state to v2, and emits a signed ACK.
  3. Due to RF interference, the ACK packet is dropped in transit.
  4. Ground M2 times out after 30 seconds and retransmits the identical packet (msg_id=42, v1 -> v2).
  5. Aircraft M4, now on v2, compares base_version=1 with its current state v2 and returns REJECTED: VERSION_MISMATCH.
  6. Outcome: Ground C2 assumes the aircraft rejected the modification and rolls back its baseline to v1. The aircraft continues navigating along the v2 path. Ground and airborne systems are now in an irrecoverable state divergence.

(5) RAND Empirical Refutation of H2/H3 and Invalidation of Scenario T13​

To validate our baseline bottleneck hypotheses H1~H4, we cross-referenced empirical combat air operation studies from RAND (NATO's Air War for Kosovo, MR-1365-AF; Air Power Against Terror, MG-166-1).

  • H1 (In-flight voice/manual relay delays) and H4 (Command approval process as primary latency bottleneck) were strongly supported by published data (MG-166 pp. 254, 294, 317; MR-1365 pp. 36, 77, 213).
  • Conversely, H2 (Ground-cockpit version desynchronization) and H3 (Inability to process partial changes forcing full rewrite pre-flight) lacked direct empirical validation in published DOD operational histories.
  • Furthermore, initial brainstorming included scenario T13 (Friendly flight breakaway due to battle damage or technical failure). Operational doctrine review revealed that T13 fell under Combat Search and Rescue (CSAR) and emergency diversion protocols rather than dynamic tactical replanning, introducing architectural inconsistency into the problem scope.

3. Deep Root Cause & Clean Fix​

To resolve these defects and doctrinal discrepancies, we overhauled the tooling pipeline, disabled kernel-level window occlusion checks, designed an idempotent transaction cache, and mapped our operational scenarios directly to official defense white papers.

(1) Isolated Headless Browser Profile & WMX Token Pipeline (Resolving D-02, D-03)​

To overcome HTTP 403 blocks and multi-download stalls, we constructed an automated acquisition pipeline utilizing isolated temporary browser profiles configured with external PDF handling:

For military specifications on ASSIST, session handshakes passing through WMX/Default.aspx?token=... one-time intermediate tokens were implemented, securing official AFDP 3-0.1 and JP 3-60 texts without data loss.

(2) Disabling Native Window Occlusion for 165Hz Telemetry (Resolving D-04, D-05)​

To prevent Chrome from throttling background rendering during headless benchmarks, we injected kernel occlusion suppression flags into the test runner:

A 10-second explicit watchdog timeout and progress indicators in the window title (document.title = "Bench [12/50]...") were coupled with the harness. As a result, 50 consecutive full-map rendering passes were completed in 25 seconds (maximum frame interval: 0.66s), achieving sustained 165Hz measurement fidelity.

(3) Idempotent Transaction Cache & State Hash Verification (Resolving B-04)​

To prevent the flight computer (M4) from rejecting valid retransmitted packets with VERSION_MISMATCH during RF dropouts, we introduced an Idempotent Transaction Cache:

# [Patched Idempotent State Machine - aircraft_sim.py]
class AircraftSim:
    def __init__(self):
        self.plan = initial_mission_plan
        self.applied_cache = {}  # msg_id -> (plan_hash, signed_ack_bytes)

    def handle_change(self, envelope):
        msg_id = envelope["body"]["msg_id"]
        base_version = envelope["body"]["base_version"]

        # 1. Idempotency Check: handle retransmissions of previously committed transactions
        if msg_id in self.applied_cache:
            cached_hash, signed_ack = self.applied_cache[msg_id]
            # Return cached signed ACK immediately if state matches post-transaction hash
            if self.calculate_plan_hash() == cached_hash:
                return signed_ack

        # 2. Sequential version consistency check
        if base_version != self.plan["version"]:
            return self.make_signed_ack(status="REJECTED", reason="VERSION_MISMATCH")

        # 3. Delta patch application and safety invariant verification
        new_plan = apply_delta(self.plan, envelope["body"]["delta"])
        if not verify_plan_invariants(new_plan):
            return self.make_signed_ack(status="REJECTED", reason="SAFETY_VIOLATION")

        # 4. Commit plan and cache signed ACK response
        self.plan = new_plan
        self.plan["version"] += 1
        signed_ack = self.make_signed_ack(status="APPLIED", new_version=self.plan["version"])
        
        self.applied_cache[msg_id] = (self.calculate_plan_hash(), signed_ack)
        return signed_ack

Figure 4: Sequence comparison between the flawed B-04 rejection behavior and the idempotent transaction cache fix. Even when ACK packets are dropped under electronic warfare jamming, retransmitted requests return cached signatures without triggering false version mismatches.

Under simulated 50% random packet drop environments, this cache architecture achieved a 100% version synchronization rate between ground and cockpit systems with zero false rejections.

(4) Grounding Scenarios T1~T12 in the 2022 Defense White Paper & Purging T13​

item.description: Overcoming the 31.4s CPython search wall (Q3) down to 0.25s, eliminating 8GB VRAM CUDA OOM via Simplex ML decoupling, and RK4 fuel accuracy verification.
item.content:encoded:
💡 Executive Summary (TL;DR)

  • The Target: Designing an end-to-end mission-critical software architecture for in-flight dynamic mission replanning (F-16 and F-15E air combat operations), generating and verifying tactical delta packages within 5.0 seconds over tactical data links (Link 16).
  • Real Engineering Pitfalls Encountered:
    1. The 31.4s CPython Search Latency Wall: Pure Python A* graph search over a 100 km × 100 km Digital Elevation Model (10^7 nodes) consumed up to 31.42 seconds (48.0s in ridge lines) due to dynamic object boxing, heap fragmentation, and runtime ray-casting, failing quality standard Q_3(<= 5.0 s).
    2. 8GB VRAM Dual-LLM CUDA OOM Trap: Loading two generative 7B/8B language models simultaneously demanded 11.44 GB VRAM (weights + KV-cache + CUDA overhead), immediately triggering torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError on single-GPU developer workstations.
    3. Ground-Truth Circularity in Fuel Metrics: Stating a "\pm 1\% calculation accuracy" without access to classified military aerodynamic polar tables created an untestable circular definition.
  • Clean Production Fixes:
    1. Pre-baked Viewshed Maps & 2D Manifold A*: Pre-computed radar lines-of-sight into a contiguous 2D float NumPy matrix during scenario loading, combining 2D horizontal A* exploration with analytical altitude clamping to slash search latency to 0.259 seconds (1/20th of the 5.0s budget).
    2. KV-Cache Elimination & 4D Cost-Weight Vectorization: Discarded generative autoregressive text generation in favor of a 0.28 GB encoder (DeBERTa-v3-small) and an MLP predicting a 4D cost vector w ∈ [0, 1]^4, reducing required VRAM to 0.80 GB (90% headroom on 8GB GPU) with zero coordinate hallucination.
    3. RK4 Numerical Ground Truth: Formulated an independent Runge-Kutta 4th Order numerical integration engine calibrated via publicly released Breguet range equations (c_0 = 0.131227 hr^{-1), achieving a maximum relative error of 3.31 × 10^{-5 to mathematically verify Q_2.

1. Target & Architecture: High-Tempo In-Flight Dynamic Replanning​

Modern aerial operations face rapidly evolving battlefields: pop-up surface-to-air missile (SAM) batteries, dynamic restricted airspace (NFZ), and time-sensitive targets (TST). In legacy strike packages, re-routing a flight requires voice coordination over tactical radios, manual coordinate transcription onto cockpit Multi-Function Displays (MFDs), and voice readbacks, creating severe tactical vulnerability.

Our engineering objective is to construct an automated, high-reliability in-flight mission replanning framework (study_for_sdc) capable of generating, validating, and transmitting graded delta mission packages over constrained tactical data links:

+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                               IN-FLIGHT DYNAMIC REPLANNING ARCHITECTURE                           |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

   [Tactical Situation C2] (M1)
              │  Mission Invalidation / Pop-up Threat / Dynamic Airspace Control (ACO)
              ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Ground Mission Authoring & Approval Node (M2)                                         │
   │   - Delta Authoring (sdc.author) & Grade Partitioning (Grade A / B / C / D)             │
   │   - Out-of-Queue Asynchronous Pre-Approval Pipeline                                    │
   │   - Canonical RFC 8785 JCS Normalization & Ed25519 Cryptographic Signing               │
   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
              │  Encoded Tactical Packets (MTU <= 1,024 Bytes)
              ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ Tactical Data Link & Satellite Simulation Layer (M3)                                   │
   │   - Link 16 (MIL-STD-6016C), MUOS Satellite, Voice Channel Modeling                   │
   │   - Deterministic Latency, Packet Loss (0~30%), and Fragment Reassembly Engine          │
   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
              │  Decoded Binary Delta Packets
              ▼
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ In-Flight Aircraft Mission Computer (M4)                                               │
   │   - Five Deterministic Safety Invariants (I1 Fuel, I2 G-Load, I3 Airspace, I4 Version) │
   │   - Deterministic Run-Time Assurance (Simplex Architecture Guard)                      │
   │   - Zero Misapplication Guarantee                                                      │
   └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The system establishes three critical technical requirements:

  • Q_3 Replanning Latency: <= 5.0 s end-to-end tactical replanning across 100 km × 100 km terrain corridors with terrain masking.
  • Local AI Execution: Must execute locally within an 8GB VRAM workstation GPU with zero OOM crashes.
  • Q_2 Calculation Accuracy: <= \pm 1.0\% relative error in time-of-arrival and fuel consumption against reference models.

During our architecture review (October 14–15), three major computational and architectural roadblocks emerged.

2. Real Errors & Pitfalls​

Pitfall 1: CPython 31.4s Search Latency Wall & Memory Thrashing (Q_3 Violation)​

Mapping a 100 km × 100 km operational radius with a 30m Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) Digital Elevation Model yields:

(100,000 m / 30 m) × (100,000 m / 30 m) ≈ 1.11 × 10^7 nodes

Even downsampling to a 100m grid with 5 discrete altitude tiers and 8 heading vectors, the 3D state space exceeds 2.5 × 10^6 nodes.

Our initial benchmark of pure CPython using the standard library heapq and dict structures collapsed under interpreter overhead:

# Raw Benchmark: Pure CPython 3D A* over 1,000,000 nodes
# Platform: Intel Core i7-13700H, 32GB RAM
Execution Wall-Clock Time: 31.42 seconds (Failed Q3: limit <= 5.0s)
Memory Allocation Overhead: 1.84 GB (Dict Hash Table & PyObject Boxing)
GIL Contention: 0% Multi-core Utilization (Single Thread Saturated)

Root Causes:

  1. Dynamic PyObject Boxing: In CPython, every integer, float, and coordinate tuple (x, y, z) is wrapped into a 28~48 byte PyObject allocated on the heap. Traversing 10^6 nodes destroyed CPU L1/L2/L3 cache locality due to pointer chasing and memory fragmentation.
  2. Dynamic Line-of-Sight (LOS) Ray-Casting: Recomputing line-of-sight from 5 threat radar emitters via Bresenham ray-casting during state expansion consumed over 70% of the entire search duration.

Pitfall 2: 8GB VRAM Dual-LLM CUDA OOM Trap​

The initial draft specification proposed hosting two 7B/8B generative LLMs (e.g., quantized Llama-3-8B Q4) on an 8GB VRAM GPU: AI-1 for grade classification and AI-2 for spatial waypoint generation.

Attempting to initialize both models triggered an immediate CUDA memory exhaustion crash:

Memory Math Breakdown:

  • Static Weights: INT4 quantization (AWQ/Q4_K_M) requires \sim 4.7 GB per 8B model. Dual models demand 4.7 × 2 = 9.4 GB.
  • KV-Cache Overhead: For a 2,048 token context window: KV-Cache = 2 × 2 × n_layers × n_heads × d_head × seq_len × bytes ≈ 0.52 GB × 2 = 1.04 GB
  • CUDA Runtime Context & Activation Buffers: \sim 1.0 GB.
  • Total Required VRAM: 9.4 + 1.04 + 1.0 = 11.44 GB (exceeding physical capacity by 43.0%).

Furthermore, autoregressive coordinate string generation produced spatial hallucinations where waypoints clipped directly through mountain ridges.

Pitfall 3: The Ground Truth Circularity Fallacy in Fuel Accuracy​

Requirement Q_2 stipulated that runtime fuel consumption calculations must achieve \pm 1.0\% accuracy.

However, classified aerodynamic drag polars and engine fuel flow tables for the F-16C Block 50 (TO 1F-16C-1-1) are classified. Stating that the software achieves "\pm 1\% accuracy relative to the actual aircraft" was an untestable circular claim without an accessible ground truth.

3. Deep Root Cause & Clean Fix​

        S1["Pre-baked Viewshed Map + 2D Manifold A*<br>(0.259s Search, Peak RAM 148MB)"]
        S2["Simplex Decoupling & Vector Embedding<br>(Total VRAM 0.80GB, KV-Cache 0MB)"]

Fix 1: Pre-Baked Viewshed Maps & 2D Manifold A* (31.4s \rightarrow 0.259s)​

We eliminated runtime ray-casting and dimensional explosion via three algorithmic optimizations:

  1. Pre-baked Viewshed Cost Matrices: Line-of-sight costs from radar emitters are pre-calculated during scenario initialization and stored in a contiguous 2D float32 NumPy array threat_cost_map[x, y]. Runtime graph expansion reads threat exposure in O(1) memory time.
  2. 2D Horizontal Manifold with Analytical Altitude Profiling: Rather than expanding a 3D lattice, the Tier 1 solver searches a 2D horizontal plane (x, y) subject to Dubins turning radius constraints (R_{min). Altitude is assigned analytically post-search by clamping between terrain elevation + Minimum Safe Distance (MSD, 500 ft) and aircraft ceiling (40,000 ft), reducing complexity from O(N^3) to O(N^2).
  3. Contiguous Memory Flat Arrays: Closed-set lookups were switched from Python dict to np.zeros(grid_shape, dtype=np.uint8), providing single-instruction cache checks.
# SDC Core Engine: Optimized 2D Grid with Pre-baked Threat Cost Lookup
def plan_route_tier1(
    grid: TerrainGrid, 
    start: Tuple[float, float], 
    goal: Tuple[float, float], 
    threat_cost_map: np.ndarray,
    turn_radius_nm: float

    # 1. Closed set managed via 1-byte flat NumPy buffer for maximum cache locality
    closed_set = np.zeros(grid.shape, dtype=np.uint8)
    
    # 2. Priority queue stores flat tuple: (f_score, h_score, x, y, heading_idx)
    open_heap = []
    heapq.heappush(open_heap, (0.0, 0.0, start[0], start[1], initial_heading))
    
    while open_heap:
        f, h, x, y, heading = heapq.heappop(open_heap)
        
        if (x, y) == goal:
            raw_path = reconstruct_path(...)
            # 3. Douglas-Peucker simplification + Dubins turn-smoothing
            smooth_path = smooth_turning_radius(raw_path, turn_radius_nm)
            return RouteResult(waypoints=smooth_path, status="SUCCESS")
            
        for dx, dy, next_heading in get_valid_maneuvers(heading, turn_radius_nm):
            nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy
            if closed_set[nx, ny]:
                continue
                
            # 4. O(1) memory lookup from pre-baked threat map (zero runtime ray-casting)
            step_cost = grid.cost[nx, ny] + threat_cost_map[nx, ny]
            # ... A* queue update

Fix 2: Technical VRAM Reduction via Simplex Decoupling (11.44GB \rightarrow 0.80GB)​

To operate within an 8GB VRAM envelope, we dismantled the generative LLM pipeline and implemented a three-tier reduction strategy under the Simplex Architecture (Sha, 2001):

               |                    UNVERIFIED COMPACT ML LAYER              |

               |   [AI-1: Grade Classifier]       [AI-2: Cost-Weight Net]    |

               |    KV-Cache: 0 MB                 KV-Cache: 0 MB             |

                                              ▼

1) Autoregressive Decoder Elimination (KV-Cache Dropped to 0 MB)​
  • Grading mission deltas (Grade A~D) is a discrete classification task, not a generative prose task.
  • By replacing autoregressive decoders with an encoder-only DeBERTa-v3-small (FP16):
    • Model weights shrank from 4.70 GB to 0.28 GB.
    • KV-Cache memory dropped from 0.52 GB to exactly 0 MB.
    • Inference latency dropped from 3,500ms to 15ms.
2) 4D Cost-Weight Vectorization Instead of Coordinate Generation​
  • Forcing models to generate coordinate strings requires billions of parameters to memorize geographic topology.
  • We restricted AI-2 strictly to predicting a 4-dimensional continuous cost weight vector: w = (α_terrain, β_threat, γ_fuel, δ_time) ∈ [0, 1]^4
  • This is executed by a lightweight 3-layer MLP requiring under 0.05 GB (50 MB) VRAM.
  • The vector w guides the deterministic A* solver, completely eliminating coordinate hallucinations.
3) Simplex Safety Decoupling​
  • Offloading physical safety guarantees (fuel margins, G-limits) to the deterministic rule engine (M2/M4) eliminated the need to encode complex safety rules into neural network parameters.

item.title: Fix Transitive npm Vulnerabilities with overrides & --omit=dev
item.description: How to resolve deep transitive dependency vulnerabilities using package.json overrides and npm audit --omit=dev without breaking your build framework.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Executive Summary (TL;DR)

  • The Problem: Running npm audit fix --force on deep transitive dependencies (packages nested inside direct dependencies) frequently forces destructive major framework downgrades, breaking modern React 19 and bundler toolchains.
  • The Solution: Declare targeted replacement rules using npm v8.3+ overrides in package.json to pin safe patch versions without waiting for upstream maintainer PR releases.
  • CI/CD Hardening: Eliminate non-production build-tool noise in GitHub Actions workflows using npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high.

1. The Transitive Dependency Nightmare​

In modern web development, your package.json direct dependencies represent only the tip of an iceberg. A typical project specifying 30 root packages frequently installs over 1,200 deeply nested transitive dependencies.

flowchart TD
    App["My React / Docusaurus App"] --> Direct["Direct Dependency: @docusaurus/core"]
    Direct --> Sub1["Sub-dependency: webpack-bundle-analyzer"]
    Sub1 --> Sub2["Transitive Dependency: ws (^7.4.0)"]
    Sub2 --> Vuln["🚨 GHSA-3h5v-q93c-6h6q (High Severity)"]

    style Vuln fill:#f87171,stroke:#dc2626,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff

When security scanners flag a vulnerability in a deeply nested leaf package (such as ws), typing npm audit fix --force triggers a destructive cascade:

  1. npm attempts to satisfy the dependency constraints of both the root framework and the nested leaf.
  2. If no official release from the intermediary maintainer exists yet, npm resolves the conflict by downgrading your entire root framework to an obsolete legacy version.
  3. This breaks build toolchains, TypeScript type definitions, and production deployment pipelines.

2. Surgical Precision: Utilizing overrides in package.json​

Starting with npm v8.3.0, developers can enforce deterministic dependency resolution across the entire dependency graph using the overrides directive.

1) Global Transitive Override​

To pin every nested instance of a vulnerable package across all dependencies:

{
  "name": "my-production-app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "dependencies": {
    "@docusaurus/core": "3.10.2"
  },
  "overrides": {
    "ws": "^8.17.1"
  }
}

2) Scoped Override (Targeting Specific Parents)​

To isolate the version bump exclusively to a specific parent package without altering other dependency trees:

{
  "overrides": {
    "webpack-bundle-analyzer": {
      "ws": "^8.17.1"
    }
  }
}

3) Cross-Ecosystem Equivalents (Yarn & pnpm)​

  • Yarn Classic (v1): Uses the resolutions field.
  • pnpm: Uses the pnpm.overrides field.
{
  "resolutions": {
    "ws": "^8.17.1"
  },
  "pnpm": {
    "overrides": {
      "ws": "^8.17.1"
    }
  }
}

3. Application & Verification Pipeline​

After adding the overrides configuration, update the lockfile and verify the resulting dependency tree:

# Step 1: Regenerate lockfile with overrides applied
npm install

# Step 2: Inspect resolution graph
npm ls ws

# Expected output:
# └─┬ @docusaurus/core@3.10.2
#   └─┬ webpack-bundle-analyzer@4.10.1
#     └── ws@8.17.1 (overridden)

# Step 3: Run security audit
npm audit

This restores a clean found 0 vulnerabilities status while preserving your top-level framework on the latest stable release.

4. CI/CD Hardening: The Power of --omit=dev​

In static sites (Docusaurus, Next.js SSG) and compiled web bundles, build-time tools (development dev servers, linters, test harnesses) never execute on production servers.

To prevent CI deployment failures caused by harmless development-time packages, restrict automated audits to production runtime artifacts:

# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
- name: Production Security Audit
  run: npm audit --omit=dev --audit-level=high

This guarantees that deployment gates monitor vulnerabilities that actually reach end-user client browsers.

5. Operational Checklist for Transitive overrides​

  1. Stay Within SemVer Minor/Patch Boundaries: Whenever possible, constrain overrides to minor or patch increments (^7.4.2 ➔ ^7.5.2). Forcing a major version bump (v7 ➔ v8) across a parent dependency that expects the old API contract can cause runtime TypeError failures during build or hydration.
  2. Prune Stale Overrides After Upstream Releases: Once the upstream parent package (e.g., @docusaurus/core or webpack-dev-server) officially updates its package.json to include the patched child dependency, remove the temporary entry from your overrides block and re-verify with npm ls <package>.

For the full threat-modeling breakdown of static site build-time vs. runtime dependencies and automated PII secret scanning, see our companion post: npm audit fix: How to Fix npm Vulnerability & GHSA Alerts.

item.title: GitHub Pages Custom Domain & Cloudflare DNS: Migration Guide
item.description: Zero-downtime migration guide for GitHub Pages custom domain with Porkbun, Cloudflare DNS, CNAME flattening, SSL edge certificates, and Docusaurus.
item.content:encoded:
Hosting an engineering blog on GitHub Pages under username.github.io/project is one of the most cost-effective and friction-free setups for developers. You push markdown files, Git workflows trigger, and GitHub serves your static artifacts worldwide.

However, operating on a shared multi-tenant subdomain (*.github.io) introduces structural limitations: it sits on the Public Suffix List (PSL), offers no custom edge HTTP security headers (HSTS, CSP, or custom cache-control rules), and ties your canonical URLs permanently to GitHub's host name rather than an infrastructure-agnostic apex domain.

To build a professional engineering presence, you need an apex custom domain (e.g., globaldevlog.com). In this first installment of our static blog infrastructure series, we walk through the exact zero-downtime migration blueprint from jbjihwan.github.io/global_blog to https://globaldevlog.com, powered by a high-availability Porkbun + Cloudflare + GitHub Pages 3-tier architecture.

1. Architectural Philosophy: The 3-Tier Production Setup​

The naive approach to connecting a custom domain to GitHub Pages is pointing raw A records from your registrar directly to GitHub's Anycast IP addresses (185.199.108.153, 185.199.109.153, 185.199.110.153, 185.199.111.153).

While functional, this legacy approach has significant operational flaws:

  • No edge DDoS protection or bot challenge filtering.
  • Slow DNS propagation when switching underlying infrastructure.
  • Zero fine-grained caching control over static assets.

We decouple responsibilities across three specialized providers:

TierProviderCore Responsibilities
1. RegistrarPorkbunLowest acquisition & annual renewal fees, perpetual free WHOIS privacy, DNSSEC
2. Edge DNS & SecurityCloudflareGlobal Anycast DNS (< 10ms resolution), CNAME Flattening on apex (@), Universal SSL, Bot Fight mode
3. Static OriginGitHub PagesPre-compiled Docusaurus artifacts, automated CI/CD via gh-pages branch, zero hosting cost

2. Step 1: Purchasing via Porkbun and Delegating NameServers​

  1. Domain Acquisition: Acquire your target .com domain on Porkbun. Porkbun offers transparent pricing with no hidden renewal markups.
  2. Add Domain to Cloudflare: Log into Cloudflare, click Add Site, enter your root domain (globaldevlog.com), and select the Free Plan.
  3. Obtain Edge Nameservers: Cloudflare assigns a dedicated pair of authoritative nameservers, for example: 
    roan.ns.cloudflare.com
    sneh.ns.cloudflare.com
  4. Delegate in Porkbun: In the Porkbun domain management dashboard:
    • Locate Authoritative Nameservers.
    • Remove Porkbun's default records (fwd0.porkbun.com, etc.).
    • Paste Cloudflare's two nameserver addresses and save. Propagation typically finishes within 5 to 15 minutes.

3. Step 2: Cloudflare CNAME Flattening & Full SSL Mode​

According to RFC 1034, an apex/naked domain (@) cannot be configured as a CNAME record because it must coexist with SOA and NS records at the zone apex. Traditionally, this forced developers to use brittle A records.

Cloudflare solves this via CNAME Flattening: at runtime, Cloudflare's edge DNS resolves the CNAME target (username.github.io) into IP addresses and returns them directly to DNS queries, providing full CNAME benefits on the naked apex.

A. Configure DNS Records​

In the Cloudflare dashboard under [DNS] > [Records], create two proxied records:

TypeNameTargetProxy StatusTTL
CNAME@jbjihwan.github.ioProxied (Orange Cloud)Auto
CNAMEwwwjbjihwan.github.ioProxied (Orange Cloud)Auto

Proxy Status Must Be Enabled: Keeping the orange cloud active routes all incoming traffic through Cloudflare's global Anycast edge, providing instant SSL termination, compression (Brotli), and automated HTTPS redirects.

B. Configure SSL/TLS Encryption​

Navigate to Cloudflare's [SSL/TLS] > [Overview]:

  • Set the encryption mode to Full (or Full Strict).
  • This ensures complete encryption across the entire route: from the user's browser to Cloudflare Edge, and from Cloudflare Edge to GitHub Pages over TLS.

4. Step 3: Docusaurus Configuration Update​

When moving from a GitHub repository subpath (e.g. /global_blog/) to an apex domain root, you must update docusaurus.config.ts:

const config: Config = {
  title: 'Global Dev Blog',
  tagline: 'Engineering Deep Dives in AI, Robotics, Computer Vision',

  // Update URL to the new apex custom domain
  url: 'https://globaldevlog.com',
  // Change baseUrl from subpath '/global_blog/' to root '/'
  baseUrl: '/',

  organizationName: 'jbjihwan',
  projectName: 'global_blog',
  trailingSlash: false,
  // ...
};

5. Step 4: The GitHub Pages CNAME Reset Trap & Solution​

One of the most maddening bugs when connecting GitHub Pages to a custom domain is the silent CNAME wipe:

  1. You enter globaldevlog.com in GitHub's repository Settings > Pages > Custom domain.
  2. You run npm run deploy from your local machine.
  3. Suddenly, your custom domain resets to username.github.io/project, and visitors get 404s or SSL certificate mismatches!

Why This Happens​

GitHub Pages expects a plain text CNAME file in the root of the deployment branch (gh-pages). When Docusaurus runs deploy, it builds fresh artifacts into build/ and force-pushes that folder to gh-pages. If the CNAME file is not inside build/, the deployment obliterates the previous CNAME commit on GitHub.

The Permanent Fix​

Place your domain directly inside static/CNAME:

globaldevlog.com

Because Docusaurus automatically copies everything in static/ to the build output root during compilation, your CNAME file is committed to gh-pages on every single release. The domain connection will never drop again.

6. Live Production Verification​

Run the deployment command:

npm run deploy

Once deployment succeeds, run quick terminal checks to verify headers and SSL certificate authenticity:

curl -I https://globaldevlog.com
# HTTP/2 200
# server: cloudflare
# strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000

curl -I https://www.globaldevlog.com
# HTTP/2 200 or 301 Redirect to apex

Summary of What We Achieved​

  • Zero Server Overhead: The entire platform runs completely free on GitHub Pages.
  • Enterprise CDN & Protection: Cloudflare absorbs traffic spikes, DDoS attempts, and manages SSL certificates automatically.
  • Canonical & Edge Independence: The domain supports full DNSSEC, custom HTTP security headers, and portable canonical URLs even if the static origin migrates in the future.

🔗 Related Infrastructure & DevSecOps Deep Dives​

  • npm audit fix: How to Fix npm Vulnerability & GHSA Alerts
  • Fix Transitive npm Vulnerabilities with overrides & --omit=dev

📌 3–5 Line Executive Summary​

  1. Architectural Cost-Efficiency: By combining Porkbun (wholesale domain registrar), Cloudflare (enterprise Anycast CDN & DNS), and GitHub Pages (zero-cost static hosting), you achieve enterprise-grade global edge distribution at $0 hosting overhead.
  2. Overcoming RFC 1034 via CNAME Flattening: Cloudflare resolves the DNS zone apex limitation by dynamically synthesizing pseudo-A records for @, allowing clean root domain routing (https://domain.com) directly to GitHub Pages.
  3. End-to-End Strict Encryption: Configuring Cloudflare SSL/TLS to 'Full (Strict)' establishes verified, bidirectional cryptographic protection from the visitor's browser all the way to GitHub's origin servers.
  4. Permanent Deployment Persistence: Hardcoding static/CNAME in Docusaurus and configuring docusaurus.config.ts prevents GitHub Pages from resetting your custom domain during automated CI/CD and deploy cycles.

item.title: npm audit fix: How to Fix npm Vulnerability & GHSA Alerts
item.description: How to run npm audit fix to resolve npm vulnerability and GHSA alerts safely without breaking your build or forcing destructive dependency downgrades.
item.content:encoded:
Every modern frontend developer has experienced this sudden spike of adrenaline: you run npm audit on your clean documentation or blog repository, and the terminal screams back in alarming red text:

45 vulnerabilities (15 moderate, 15 high, 15 critical)
To address all issues (including breaking changes), run:
  npm audit fix --force

Seeing words like Critical, Remote Code Execution (RCE), and Prototype Pollution triggers an immediate instinct: type npm audit fix --force to make the scary red warnings go away.

However, in the world of Static Site Generators (SSG) like Docusaurus, Next.js, or Hugo deployed to GitHub Pages or AWS S3, doing so is often an engineering mistake that breaks production builds without improving your actual security posture.

In this article, we dissect the static site threat model, explain why bundler vulnerabilities differ fundamentally from server vulnerabilities, and share a production-tested 4-Layer Security Hardening Blueprint to protect what actually matters: your secrets, client privacy, and repository integrity.

1. Executive Summary: The Core Engineering Trade-off​

  1. Build-Time Tools != Production Runtime: Packages flagged in npm audit (such as tinypool, serialize-javascript, postcss-selector-parser) are node worker and bundler dependencies executed locally on your machine during npm run build.
  2. Zero Live Server on CDN: Once compiled, GitHub Pages serves static, immutable HTML, CSS, and client-side JavaScript. There is no running Node.js daemon, no backend port listening, and no database connection in production.
  3. The Danger of --force: Running npm audit fix --force blindly downgrades core frameworks (e.g., rolling Docusaurus back to older releases), breaking React 19 compatibility, MDX v3 pipelines, and future flag architectures.
  4. Where Real Static Risks Lie: The genuine security risks of static blogs are credential/API key leakage in public Git history, PII exposure in datasets, and client-side cross-origin leakage.

2. Anatomy of the 45 Vulnerabilities: Build vs Runtime​

Let's examine the actual CVEs reported in our audit log:

A. Tinypool Prototype Pollution (GHSA-5gmw-xhrv-c9v3 - Critical)​

  • Vulnerability: If untrusted user input is passed into the worker initialization options of tinypool, an attacker can pollute Object.prototype.
  • Reality in SSG: tinypool is used internally by @docusaurus/faster to parallelize bundling tasks across CPU cores during build time. The input parameters come solely from your own docusaurus.config.ts. No external visitor on your website can send HTTP payloads to your local CPU worker pool.

B. Serialize-JavaScript RCE (GHSA-5c6j-r48x-rmvq - High)​

  • Vulnerability: Remote Code Execution via crafted RegExp flags or serialized dates.
  • Reality in SSG: Webpack uses this to serialize internal compilation chunks into static .js bundles. Once written to the build/ directory, JavaScript files are passive assets served over HTTPS. No server-side deserialization takes place.

C. PostCSS Selector Parser CPU Exhaustion (GHSA-rj75-hqrm-r3gf - Moderate)​

  • Vulnerability: Quadratic complexity in flat selector parsing allows Denial of Service (DoS) via maliciously crafted CSS strings.
  • Reality in SSG: The CSS files being parsed are your own theme stylesheets (custom.css). Unless an attacker has write access to your Git repository, your build server will never parse untrusted external CSS.

Running npm audit fix --force in this situation attempts to downgrade @docusaurus/core from 3.10.2 to 3.7.0. This breaks Docusaurus v4 future flags and React 19 rendering, introducing breaking bugs into your codebase to patch an exploit that cannot physically occur in your architecture.

3. What Actually Matters: The 4-Layer Static Security Blueprint​

If npm bundler vulnerabilities are low risk, where should static site engineers invest their security budget? Here is the multi-layered defense pipeline implemented in this blog.

Layer 1: Automated Pre-Commit Secret Scanning​

The single greatest catastrophic risk for public technical blogs is accidentally committing an OpenAI key (sk-...), a GitHub Personal Access Token (ghp_...), or an AWS access credential (AKIA...).

We created an automated audit script (tools/audit_security.py) that utilizes Git's object database to scan every tracked file against high-entropy regex patterns:

PATTERNS = [
    (r'(?i)(api[_-]?key|secret|token|password|auth|bearer)\s*[:=]\s*["\']([^"\']{8,})["\']', "Potential Key Assignment"),
    (r'ghp_[a-zA-Z0-9]{36}', "GitHub Personal Access Token"),
    (r'sk-[a-zA-Z0-9]{32,}', "OpenAI API Key"),
    (r'AIzaSy[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{33}', "Google API Key"),
    (r'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}', "AWS Access Key"),
    (r'-----BEGIN\s+(RSA\s+)?PRIVATE\s+KEY-----', "Private Key Certificate"),
]

Running this audit script before every release ensures zero hardcoded tokens ever reach the remote repository.

Layer 2: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) Scrubbing​

When publishing engineering articles on AI datasets (such as our 23-part Maeumjigi conversational AI series or 5-part ANPR Vision AI series):

  • Synthetic Data First: All counseling records were synthetically generated via LLM pipelines (synth_gen) rather than using real clinical transcripts, guaranteeing zero medical privacy breach.
  • Regex PII Audit: Our scanner automatically validates markdown text against Korean national identity numbers (\d{6}-[1-4]\d{6}) and phone numbers (010-\d{4}-\d{4}).

Layer 3: Hardened .gitignore Configuration​

A standard .gitignore often ignores .env.local while leaving .env exposed. We hardened .gitignore to comprehensively block sensitive files, private certificates, and raw analytics dumps:

# Environment & Secret Protection
.env
.env.*
*.pem
*.key
*.pfx
*.cert
*credential*
*.secret

# Analytics & CSV dumps
*.csv

# Archived template files
_old/

Layer 4: Client-Side Privacy & Iframe Sandboxing​

Even without a backend server, static sites must respect user privacy and prevent data leakage:

  1. Strict Referrer Policy: In docusaurus.config.ts, we inject a strict referrer header into <head>:

    themeConfig: {
      metadata: [
        { name: 'referrer', content: 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' },
      ],
    }

    This ensures that when a reader clicks an external documentation link, your blog's specific full URL parameters are truncated, preventing path leakage.

  2. Giscus Discussion Sandboxing: We host comments via GitHub Discussions. In BlogPostItem/index.tsx, Giscus is configured with:

    • emitMetadata="0": Prevents post-message iframe broadcasts from exposing discussion details to third-party browser scripts.
    • loading="lazy": Prevents iframe resource execution until the reader scrolls to the bottom of the article.

4. Key Takeaways for Developers​

  • Do Not Panic at npm audit: Always distinguish between Build-Time Bundler Dependencies and Production Runtime Dependencies.
  • Beware of --force: Automated downgrades often introduce real, breaking application bugs while solving theoretical vulnerabilities that cannot be triggered on a static CDN.
  • Focus on the Real Attack Surface: Automate secret detection, scrub sensitive data from datasets, enforce strict client-side referrer policies, and protect your Git history.

item.title: [Vision AI] Korean ANPR OCR Engine, Regex Normalization & Temporal Majority Voting (v01 to v11 Evolution) (#5)
item.description: Korean license plate syntax validation, EasyOCR tuning, temporal sliding window majority voting, and the complete 11-iteration engineering journey from v01 to v11.
item.content:encoded:
📌 Key Takeaways (TL;DR)

  • Problem: Single-frame OCR inevitably suffers from transient misreadings (e.g., 64아1511, 24가1511) due to vehicle yaw, glare, and vibration.
  • Solution: Implemented Korean plate regex validation (^\d{2,3}[가-힣]\d{4}$) coupled with a temporal sliding window majority voting engine across a 7-frame buffer (plate_confirm_threshold=3).
  • Result: Advanced through 11 system iterations (v01 to v11), transitioning from initial gibberish (ACCIIXOY-1Z01...) on June 5 to deterministic confirmation of 64가1511 on June 7 with 99.4% reliability.

1. Korean ANPR Syntax & EasyOCR Tuning​

Korean vehicle registration plates follow strict regulatory syntax:

Syntax: [2 or 3 Digits] + [1 Hangul Syllable] + [4 Digits]
Example: 64가1511, 123가4567
import easyocr
import re
from collections import deque, Counter

reader = easyocr.Reader(['ko', 'en'], gpu=True)

def parse_korean_plate(plate_img):
    results = reader.readtext(plate_img, detail=0)
    raw_text = "".join(results).replace(" ", "")
    
    # Korean License Plate Regex Match
    pattern = r'(\d{2,3}[가-힣]\d{4})'
    match = re.search(pattern, raw_text)
    return match.group(1) if match else None

2. Temporal Majority Voting Engine​

To overcome transient single-frame OCR flicker, we maintain a sliding history queue:

plate_history = deque(maxlen=CONFIG["plate_history_size"])  # 7
confirmed_plate = None

def update_plate_voting(detected_text):
    global confirmed_plate
    if detected_text:
        plate_history.append(detected_text)
        
    if len(plate_history) >= CONFIG["plate_confirm_threshold"]:
        counts = Counter(plate_history)
        most_common_plate, count = counts.most_common(1)[0]
        
        # Confirm plate if 3 or more votes agree
        if count >= CONFIG["plate_confirm_threshold"]:
            confirmed_plate = most_common_plate
            
    return confirmed_plate

3. The 11-Iteration Evolution: June 5 to June 7​

Our log.txt preserves the raw chronological milestones:

TimestampRaw Plate LogTechnical Iteration & Key Breakthrough
06-05 01:13ACCIIXOY-1Z01V1t145V...v01: Unconstrained full-frame OCR. Road textures misinterpreted as text
06-06 00:13fa이, ealan, caiv04: YOLOv3 vehicle bounding box integration
06-06 01:4064115114, 16416114v07: Dedicated YOLOv5 plate detector crops plate ROI
06-06 16:3564아1511 -> 64가1511v09: EDSR_x4 deep super-resolution resolves Hangul stroke
06-07 01:2724가1511 -> 64가1511v10: Multi-frame image stacking cancels sensor noise
06-07 18:2064가1511 (Size: 370x315)v11 Final: Temporal Majority Voting locks deterministic plate confirmation!

4. Real Runtime Errors & Debugging Log​

Bug 1: EasyOCR Re-initialization Memory Leak (850MB VRAM Spike per Event)​

In v07, easyocr.Reader(['ko', 'en'], gpu=True) was instantiated inside the violation callback function. Every lane intrusion event reloaded the CRAFT detector and Korean recognition CRNN weights onto the GPU, adding ~850MB of CUDA allocations and crashing after 8 vehicles with torch.cuda.OutOfMemoryError.

  • Fix: Moved easyocr.Reader(['ko'], gpu=True) to a module-level singleton initialized once at startup, and restricted allowlist="0123456789가나다라마거너더러머버서어저고노도로모보소오조구누두루무부수우주아바사자배하허호" so the decoder never wastes probability mass on non-license-plate Hangul syllables or Latin letters.

Bug 2: Global confirmed_plate State Bleed Across Consecutive Vehicles​

Using a single global plate_history = deque(maxlen=7) caused votes from Vehicle #1 (64가1511) to bleed into Vehicle #2's buffer when two cars crossed the lane within 2 seconds.

  • Fix: Keyed plate_history by CSRT track_id (dict[int, deque]) and purged stale tracker IDs after 30 frames of inactivity.

5. Conclusion & Future Horizons​

Across this 5-part series, we designed an end-to-end computer vision system integrating dynamic lane tracking, polygon IoU intrusion detection, hierarchical object localization, CSRT tracking, EDSR_x4 super-resolution, and temporal voting OCR. This pipeline provides a proven template for production-grade intelligent transportation systems.

📌 3–5 Line Executive Summary​

  1. Korean License Plate Syntax Validation: EasyOCR character output is strictly filtered against standardized Korean plate regex patterns (^\d{2,3}[가-힣]\d{4}$), discarding syntactically invalid character fragments.
  2. Temporal Sliding Window Majority Voting: To counteract frame-level yaw, glare, and vibration, OCR hypotheses are buffered across a 7-frame sliding window, requiring 3 identical matches before confirming the plate.
